strategy.summary: Small private Hungarian laser/sheet-metal shop (Kft., 90 staff, financially sound), single approved source on part:330040 (inox control cabinet housing HI) under a framework agreement with yearly fixed prices and an open renewal exit; we own the tooling. It has idle capacity (second shift on hold) and asked for faster payment, so volume and cash are its currencies. Its delivery and quality have slipped badly, and it has historically settled below its ask. Over the last year, its cost drivers (alloy 1.4301, steel, labour) moved in its favour, although alloy has recently eased. There is modest room on price, reached mainly through trades. Do not squeeze hard: it is our only source and is already underperforming. Evidence on cost structure, people and margin is thin (no should-cost, no named contacts).
strategy.decision_maker: Unknown. Likely the sales contact together with the owner-manager of a small private Kft.; no sign of a deep approval ladder (sup:70330, doc:20260206-70330-M1). Evidence on named people is missing.

persona.style: Accommodating and pragmatic. Opens with small asks and settles below them. Communicates in a formal, planned way.
other_traits: financially sound, can afford to walk away
recurring wrong material certificates point to a process weakness
we are about 8 % of its turnover
we pay invoices slightly late, which gives it a counter-grievance

needs.detail: The second shift has been on hold, and it offered to take additional parts at short notice. Binding volume or added parts are worth more to it than they cost us.
It asked for payment within short days in exchange for a cash discount. This reads as a utilisation and liquidity squeeze, not distress.
Our forecast is rising and has been shared with it. It values planned, binding volume.
A longer commitment via auto-extension or a 24-month term protects its loading.
The 1.4301 alloy surcharge and steel producer prices rose over the last twelve months, so it may ask for cost recovery or an alloy clause.

constraints.detail: Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice ahead of year end, so an increase outside the notice window has no contractual basis.
It is the only approved source at a full quota. We own the tooling, but requalification time is unknown.
Delivery and quality are deteriorating: late confirmations against our requested dates and recurring certificate errors. Pressing too hard on margin could worsen this.
Plant closes over the year-end holidays, so January call-offs must be placed early.

levers.why: Rising, shared forecast for a supplier with idle machines; the strongest price lever.
Its own statement on idle capacity makes extra or binding volume worth a price step; it should be paired with the volume offer.
Anchors any discussion at the current price.
Checkable recent alloy fall that offsets part of its alloy-rise claim.
Rolling ppm is far above the peer median and the prior year; it undercuts any increase and supports a ppm commitment.
On-time delivery is far below target. Use it as a fresh fact in a later round, framed as performance against our requested date.
Part-specific complaints, including repeated certificate errors. Use as a fresh record and as the basis for a ppm or chargeback trade.
Fixed yearly price with a notice requirement; only relevant if it asks late or mid-year.
Use internally to calibrate expectations. Cite only if it insists on its ask.
Quiet reminder that resourcing is feasible. Use only if it hardens; never as a threat.
Contractual on-time-delivery target it is missing; supports a quality and delivery package.

trades.why: It explicitly asked for faster payment; give shorter terms in exchange for a price step, ideally in the last round.
Idle second shift: commit binding volume within our real need (forecasts are volatile) for a price step.
Planning security for a shop needing load; 24 months captures the value, 36 adds nothing.
Tight ppm target as the quality repair it should accept; secure it first in quality cases.
The current flat fee barely covers handling. Test it as a trade rather than dropping it.
Do not ask for shorter lead times while it confirms late. Fit its own lead time and secure adherence instead.
The alloy index has risen over twelve months, so a clause now would mainly raise our cost. Accept one only if it insists and the clause is priced well below the fixed price.

price_view.reasoning: There is no should-cost, so the margin is unknown. Over twelve months the drivers support a moderate increase claim, partly offset by the recent alloy dip. Long-term peaks favour us but are not checkable. The price has already fallen markedly since 2023, and it settled below its ask in every renewal. Holding the current price is realistic; a small cut is possible only through trades: faster payment, binding volume and a 24-month term. Poor performance weakens any increase.

do: Acknowledge its payment request explicitly and answer it with an offer.
Commit to paying on time; we have been paying slightly late.
Frame volume growth and the second shift as a shared opportunity.
Raise quality and delivery factually, with rolling scorecard figures, as a joint fix.
Make a real, shrinking step each round, paired with a fresh record or trade.
dont: Do not threaten resourcing or termination, or set deadlines.
Do not ask open questions about its costs or margin.
Do not cite copper, electronics or 1.4404 news, or long-term peak figures, as checkable facts.
Do not ask for 60-90 day payment while it wants cash.
Do not counter below a declared final offer.

traps: Citing the 36-month or all-time alloy and steel peak arguments (not checkable; costs trust).
Using the tooling or exit window as a threat against our only source.
Pushing payment terms longer while we pay late: it will raise our late-payment record (payment_behaviour:all:11829f07).
Giving shorter payment mid-negotiation, where it is absorbed into a normal step.
Committing volume above our real need; forecasts have swung.
Accepting an alloy index clause on a rising index at a generous price.
Per-lot ppm figures: use the rolling scorecard ppm instead.
Squeezing margin hard while quality and delivery are already slipping.
strategy.writer_notes: Open with the rising forecast and its own wish to load the second shift. Offer binding volume and a longer term. Anchor at the current price and cite the recent alloy dip. Keep shorter payment as the closing trade, and say we will pay on time. Bring quality and delivery in as fresh facts in later rounds, alongside a ppm commitment, in a cooperative tone. Evidence on cost structure and decision makers is thin; avoid margin claims. Watch the contract notice window for price changes and plan January call-offs around the holiday shutdown.

findings.text: No should-cost and no competing quotes exist for part 330040, so we cannot say how far 119.11 sits above full cost; margin room can only be inferred from drivers and price history. Evidence is thin on the cost side.

Weighted 12-month driver movement favours the supplier: LCI-C +2.7% (w0.29, ~+0.77%), AS-14301 +8.6% (w0.23, ~+1.99%), PPI-C241 +6.5% (w0.14, ~+0.92%), together about +3.7% on price for the 66% of cost covered. The remaining 34% has no driver assigned. This is the size of increase it can credibly assert at the next renewal.

Against that, the drivers are well below their 2022-2023 peaks: AS-14301 is -17.6% vs its 36-month peak and -44.9% vs its 2022 high, and PPI-C241 is -6.3% and -26.7% respectively. The 2023 price of 132.01 was set in a dearer cost environment. The cuts to 119.11 (-9.8%) only partly track the alloy fall, so the cumulative cost picture since 2023 is roughly neutral to slightly in our favour. However, these peak comparisons are not checkable; use them only as context.

Short-term alloy surcharge reversal: AS-14301 has fallen 7.6% since 2026-06, about -1.76% on price. This is the one checkable recent driver argument for us, and it offsets about half of the 12-month alloy rise.

Price history: 132.01 (2023), 122.14 (2024, -7.5%), 122.14 (2025), 119.11 (2026, -2.5%). The supplier has settled below its ask in each of 3 renewals (average ask +0.3%, settled -3.3%). Last time it asked +1.5% and settled -2.5%, while labour and steel were already rising.

Room on price looks modest. Holding 119.11 is defensible given the recent alloy dip, the volume rise to 2910 and its poor performance (70.8% on-time delivery, 1879 ppm). A further cut of about 1-2% is possible, mainly through trades: faster payment, which it has asked for, and volume. Pushing much below that risks a single source with spare capacity and a sound balance sheet walking away.
Market news on copper (+48%) and electronic boards (+41%) is irrelevant to this inox laser part. If the supplier cites it, rebut it. The 1.4404 surcharge news concerns a different grade.

findings.text: Small, privately owned Hungarian laser/sheet-metal shop (90 staff, ~EUR 3.9 M turnover). Decisions likely sit with sales and the owner-manager, with no deep approval ladder. The evidence on people is thin: no named contacts and no meeting notes on decision makers.

Under-utilised capacity: sales said they could take extra parts at short notice and that the second shift has been on hold since spring. They need volume. Added or bundled parts, or binding volume, are worth more to them than price.

Values cash: they asked for payment within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount. Faster payment is a strong currency to trade against price. Weak spot: we pay late on 92.8% of invoices (avg 3.8 days, max 11), which they can raise.

Financially stable rather than stressed: equity ratio 35.3%, credit index 248 unchanged over 12 months, VDA 6.3 grade B. The cash request plus the idle shift suggest a utilisation squeeze, not distress. Their margin is probably not critical, but the evidence on margin is thin.

We are a meaningful customer: about 8.2% of their turnover (EUR 320k in FY2026). Planned volume is rising (2910 units against 2658). They are single source on part 330040, but we own the tooling, so dependency runs both ways.

Performance has slipped badly, which weakens their stance. Rolling quality is 1879 ppm against a peer median of 457 (396 a year ago), from 5 complaints including a wrong material certificate. On-time delivery is 70.8% against the 95% target (84.6% a year earlier). All 8Ds are closed.

Negotiation history: they open with small asks and settle well below them (last round asked +1.5%, settled -2.5%). The price fell from 132.01 to 119.11 since 2023. They are accommodating, but further cuts have diminishing room.
Operational style: formal, planned communication. Plant closed 23 Dec to 6 Jan, with January call-offs requested by 10 Dec.

findings.text: Framework agreement covers only part:330040 (control cabinet housing HI); prices fixed per calendar year, changes need written notice at least 90 days before year end (i.e. by ~2 Oct for 2027). Payment 60 days net, FCA, lead time 35 days.
Term runs to 2027-06-30 and auto-extends 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice (by 2027-04-01); exit remains open and credible because we own the tooling.

Quality agreement: OTD target 95 %, EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint. Supplier is clearly below: 70.8 % on time (84.6 % a year earlier), 1879 ppm vs peer median 457, 5 complaints on this part (EUR 750 recharged).

History: three renewals asked +0.3 % on average and settled -3.3 %; last renewal asked +1.5 %, settled -2.5 %; 2024 asked +3.2 %, settled 0. Price fell 132.01 -> 119.11 (-9.8 %) since 2023. It reliably moves below its ask, though steps are shrinking.

Mutual dependency: 100 % quota, single approved source since 2019 (supply risk for us), but we own the tooling and represent ~8.2 % of its EUR 3.89 M turnover; spend growing (EUR 265k -> 320k) and volume forecast up (2910 vs 2658). Supplier has idle capacity (second shift on hold) and asked for faster payment, signalling cash/volume need. Financially sound (equity 35.3 %, credit index 248 stable).
Our weakness: we pay on average 3.8 days late (92.8 % of invoices late) — they can raise this against us.

findings.text: Delivery is deteriorating steadily: on-time vs requested date fell from 88.5% (2025Q2) to 70.8% in the rolling 12 months to 2026-09, against a 95% contract target and a peer median of 84.6%. Against its own confirmed date it stays at ~92%, so the problem is that it confirms later than we request, not that it misses its promises. Late receipts average 12.6 days, max 25.

Quality has worsened sharply: rolling ppm rose from 396 a year ago to 1879 (peer median 457), with 5 supplier-caused complaints in 12 months, all on part:330040. Wrong material certificate recurred three times (2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-05), so the 8D actions did not hold. 8Ds are closed and none overdue, but closure is slowing (d8 up to ~3 months). Scorecard dropped from class A green to B amber (score 76).

Direct cost recovered is small: EUR 150 flat fee per complaint, EUR 750 in the last 12 months (EUR 900 total), which barely covers handling; our true cost of 29% late receipts and returns is not recharged. This argues for a price or terms concession, or a tighter ppm/chargeback commitment, rather than only fees.

Volume outlook is positive for the supplier: forecast for the next 12 months is 2910 pcs vs 2658 ordered in the last 12 months (+9.5%), shared with it; at ~119 EUR that is roughly EUR 345k a year, about 8-9% of its EUR 3.9 M turnover. It has spare capacity (second shift on hold), so the extra volume is valuable to it. Note: our forecasts have been volatile (2576-3150) and the June 2026 peak of 3150 was cut, so do not oversell commitment.

Price history favours us as an anchor (we now pay 119.11, down from 132.01 in 2023 and 122.14 in 2024-25) but the supplier can argue it has already cut 9.8%. Order behaviour is stable, with a few rush lines (3) and late confirmations (8 lines confirmed later than requested), e.g. the 2026-09-14 order confirmed 12 days late.
Evidence is limited to one part (part:330040, single source, 100% quota) with ~24 receipts a year, so per-lot ppm is jumpy; the rolling scorecard ppm is the fairer figure to cite.

arguments.text: Our cost drivers have risen materially over twelve months. The 1.4301 alloy surcharge is +8.6% year on year, steel producer prices are +6.5%, and labour is +2.7%. Weighted by the category team's own estimates, this alone is roughly +3.5% on the part cost. Yet our price has fallen 9.8% since 2023, from 132.01 to 119.11. Holding the current price is already a concession; an increase of about 3% is justified.

weak_points: Delivery has slipped badly: on time against requested dates is down to 70.8% from 91.1% score-class A, ppm is 1879 and the scorecard is now class B amber. This undercuts any increase.
There are recurring wrong material certificates (three of them), which is a process failure, not a cost issue.
Idle capacity: we told them the second shift has been on hold and that we could take parts at short notice. This shows we need volume.
Our cash request reveals liquidity interest.
Historically we settled below our ask every year, so they expect us to fold.
The alloy surcharge fell 7.6% within the year and is 17.6% below its 36-month peak; steel is below its 2023 peak.
Industrial power is -43% versus 2022, which matters for a laser shop.
Under clause 3.1, any increase needs written notice 90 days before year end. If we are late, there is no contractual basis.
Our customer's forecast fell from 3150 to 2910.
wants: Payment within 10 days, with a 2% cash discount offered in return; this is the most valuable lever for us.
A binding annual volume of at least about 2900 pcs, or additional parts to fill the second shift; for this we would give a price cut of 1-2%.
A 24-month term or a renewed auto-extension, worth holding the price flat.
Alternatively, an alloy index clause on AS-14301 at a 0.23 weight instead of a fixed increase.
A lower chargeback, or no ppm commitment, in exchange for a corrective action plan.
red_lines: No price cut beyond about 3% in total, even with all trades; our margin is unknown, and the business is small at 3.9 M turnover.
No price cut without a payment or volume trade.
No hard ppm commitment with high per-complaint chargebacks while certificate issues are being fixed.
No lead time below 35 days without binding call-offs.
No Incoterm change to delivered (DAP/DDP) at the current price.
red_team.opening: Thank our customer for six years of partnership and acknowledge openly that delivery and certificate quality fell short this year, presenting a corrective plan (certificate double-check, buffer stock). Then show the driver data (alloy +8.6%, steel +6.5%, labour +2.7%) against our price, which has fallen 9.8% since 2023. Ask for +2.9% from January, and immediately offer an alternative: hold the price if they pay in 10 days with a 2% discount, or commit to 24 months and binding volume. Make concessions in shrinking steps.

rebuttals.answer: We agree that the alloy surcharge, steel producer prices and labour costs have risen over the past twelve months, and we do not dismiss that. The full picture matters, though. The alloy surcharge has also fallen noticeably within that same year, so part of the rise has already reversed. The weighted effect on the part therefore sits below the figure you quote. The reductions since the first contract price came out of our yearly renewals, which both sides agreed. They also reflected the volume we have placed with you, which has grown steadily. Our current order price is the right basis for this discussion. Over the same period, on-time delivery against our requested dates and the complaint rate have both moved clearly the wrong way. That makes an increase hard to justify internally. We would rather work on what helps you most: more binding volume to load your capacity, a longer commitment, and faster payment. Together with a joint plan on quality and delivery, these can keep the price where it is, which is fair to both of us.

press: Our forecast for the coming year, which we have shared with you, is above what we ordered last year, and we would gladly commit part of it as binding volume to help fill your second shift.
You asked about faster payment, and we are open to shortening our terms as part of an overall agreement; we will also make sure invoices are paid on time.
Delivery against our requested dates has dropped noticeably over the last year, and we would like to agree a joint plan to bring it back toward the contractual target.
The repeated wrong material certificates look like a process issue rather than a cost issue, and we would value a systemic fix together with a ppm commitment.
The alloy surcharge has eased again in recent months, so part of the yearly rise you cite has already reversed.
Under our framework agreement, prices are fixed per calendar year, and any change needs timely written notice, so we would like to handle this within that process.

arguments.note: ctr:4600070330#5.1 (delivery): Delivery FCA; standard lead time 35 days from order.

arguments.sentence: Our framework agreement includes the quality agreement with its delivery target.
arguments.note: ctr:4600070330#6.1 (quality): The quality agreement applies: on-time delivery target 95 %, flat fee of EUR 150 per supplier-caused complaint.

arguments.sentence: Our framework agreement renews only unless either side gives notice.
arguments.note: ctr:4600070330#8.1 (term): Valid from 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30; extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice. To stop the renewal, notice by 2027-04-01 (still open: a credible exit).
